Study on recycling of ZM6 rare-earth magnesium alloy scrap by vacuum sublimation gasification

Highlights

  • •
    Proposed vacuum sublimation gasification process for recycling ZM6 scrap, tackling environmental risks and RE-metal loss.
  • •
    The feasibility of separating and recycling Mg and Nd from ZM6 alloy scrap by vacuum sublimation gasification was evaluated.
  • •
    Achieved 99.936 % Mg and 83.84 % Nd purity under optimized conditions, proving this recycling process potential.
  • •
    Provides a novel pathway to enhance circular economy practices for Mg alloys and maximize rare earth element recovery.

Abstract

Magnesium (Mg) alloys have great potential for lightweight use and are widely applied in automotive industry. Rare earth magnesium (RE-Mg) alloys, enhanced with rare earth (RE) elements, and their superior properties enable their expanded application in key aerospace components. However, the stringent requirements in aerospace applications lead to lower production yields, inevitably generating a significant amount of RE-containing Mg alloy scrap. Traditional recycling methods risk environmental harm and loss of valuable RE elements. This study proposes a vacuum sublimation gasification process for recycling Mg and neodymium (Nd) from ZM6 RE magnesium alloy. Through thermodynamic analysis, the feasibility of separating and recycling Mg and Nd was evaluated, along with its separation capacity, and the content and behavior of elements in the gas phase were predicted. Experimental results confirm that vacuum sublimation gasification is thermodynamically viable. Under optimal gasification conditions—pressure of 10 Pa, gasification temperature of 750 °C, and holding time of 120 min—recycled Mg with a purity of 99.936 wt% and Nd with a purity of 83.84 wt% were obtained. This research provides novel ideas and guidance for enhancing the sustainable circulation of Mg and maximizing the utilization of RE resources.

1. Introduction

Magnesium (Mg) alloys represent the lightest structural metallic materials in practical applications. Owing to their high specific strength and stiffness, excellent castability, damping and noise reduction properties, electromagnetic shielding capability, machinability, and recyclability [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]], they have been widely used in transportation, telecommunications, electronics, and aerospace industries, particularly in automotive lightweighting [[6], [7], [8]]. However, their low strength at both ambient and elevated temperatures, poor creep resistance and insufficient corrosion resistance significantly limit their application in more demanding aerospace environments [[9], [10], [11]]. The addition of rare earth (RE) elements to form rare earth magnesium (RE-Mg) alloys can significantly enhance their mechanical properties, such as fatigue and wear resistance, corrosion resistance [[12], [13], [14], [15]]. Among RE elements, neodymium (Nd) is more cost-effective than gadolinium (Gd) and dysprosium (Dy), making Nd-containing RE-Mg alloys more favorable for practical applications [16]. Among these alloys, ZM6, a high-strength heat-resistant Mg alloy containing Nd elements, was successfully developed by China in 1980 and started to be used in production. It exhibits excellent creep resistance, endurance strength, and instantaneous tensile properties at elevated temperatures up to 250 °C [17,18]. Hence, ZM6 alloy has been widely applied in the aerospace industry for manufacturing critical load-bearing components, such as aircraft wing ribs and hydraulic constant-speed device brackets [[19], [20], [21]].
Typically, the yield of conventional Mg alloy castings is only around 50 % [22], while the stringent service conditions in the aerospace and military industry sectors further reduce the yield of RE-Mg alloy components. According to the information provided by a relevant parts supplier, the production of 1 t qualified parts requires approximately 10 t of RE-Mg alloy raw materials. This inevitably produces a large amount of RE-Mg alloy scrap. However, due to technical limitations, it is difficult for component manufacturers to reuse these scraps, and it is often sold at a low price as ordinary Mg alloy scrap, without pricing RE elements, to specialized recyclers, which significantly reduces the economic efficiency. Furthermore, traditional flux recycling methods result in significant burn-off of RE elements, leading to the loss of valuable RE resources and environmental pollution [23,24]. Currently, only a few reports have been reported on the use of solid-state recycling methods to recycle such RE-Mg alloy scrap, in which alloy scrap is ball-milled under a protective atmosphere or processed into chips through machining, followed by compaction and deformation processing to manufacture recycled alloy billets [[25], [26], [27]]. Solid-state recycling is currently the most economical and environmentally friendly recycling method, but there are still many challenges before commercialization [28]. Therefore, developing an efficient approach for recovering both Mg and RE elements from RE-Mg alloys is a critical challenge. It would not only reduce manufacturing costs for producers but also maximize the recycling of valuable metals, contributing to sustainable resource utilization.
Vacuum gasification has emerged as a highly efficient, environmentally friendly, and technologically simple method, and has been widely used in alloy separation, metal purification and secondary metal resources recycling [[29], [30], [31], [32]], which demonstrates significant potential in the recycling of Mg alloy scrap. The distinctive thermodynamic characteristics of Mg, its elevated vapor pressure at melting conditions (376 Pa at the triple point), enable Mg to easily undergo a sublimation phase transformation mechanism (solid→gas), which differs from most non-ferrous metals when the pressure lower this critical pressure. During this process, Mg transitions directly from solid to gas, compared with vacuum distillation, not only lowering the gasification temperature but also achieving a faster evaporation rate, thereby leading to a higher recovery efficiency. Therefore, this study proposed a new process of vacuum sublimation gasification to recycle metal Mg and Nd from RE-Mg alloy ZM6. The feasibility of this process was discussed from the thermodynamic aspect. Through a combination with the experimental study, the optimal recycling conditions for achieving high-purity recycled metal Mg and Nd enrichment were obtained. The objective is to maximize the utilization and circulation of Mg and RE metal resources in the most economically viable manner, thereby enhancing resource efficiency and sustainability.

2. Materials and methods

The ZM6 (Mg–Nd–Zn) alloy scrap used in this study was provided by a Mg alloy parts manufacturer in Anhui province of China, and its chemical composition is shown in Table 1. Fig. 1 presents the physical appearance and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the ZM6 alloy scrap. As observed in Fig. 1(b), the microstructure of ZM6 consists of an α-Mg solid solution (dark regions) and eutectic compounds Mg12(Nd,Zn) (bright regions) distributed along the grain boundaries. The dense interlacing flake precipitation in the crystal was formed during the aging treatment, primarily consisting of the dispersion-precipitated enhanced phase Mg12(Nd,Zn) [17,21,33]. The Mg12(Nd,Zn) with a small amount of Zn in solid solution has stronger thermal stability than Mg12Nd compounds, thus improving the high temperature performance of ZM6 alloy. Additionally, some zirconium (Zr)-containing particles are present, which play a crucial role in grain refinement [34]. Hence, as shown in Fig. 1(c), Nd, Zn, and Zr are uniformly distributed throughout the Mg matrix.

The vacuum sublimation gasification equipment used in this study is a horizontal tube furnace, consisting of a heating zone, a condensation zone, and a vacuum system. A schematic diagram of the equipment setup and mechanism is shown in Fig. 2. A 70 ± 0.5 g sample of scrap material was placed into a graphite crucible and inserted into a quartz tube (length: 1200 mm, diameter: 50 mm, wall thickness: 3 mm), with high-purity graphite paper (thickness: 0.3 mm) lining the inner wall of the quartz tube to collect condensates. The crucible was positioned at the center of the heating zone, and after sealing the apparatus, the vacuum pump (Value VRI-8, ultimate pressure: 0.2 Pa, volume flow rate: 8.0 m3/h) was activated. Once the vacuum pressure reached 10 Pa, the system was heated at a rate of 10 K/min according to the preset program. Upon reaching the target gasification temperature (700–900 °C), the sample was held at a constant temperature for a specified duration. Upon heating, metallic Mg in the heating zone undergoes gasification, forming metal vapor. Driven by both the concentration of metal vapor and temperature gradients, the vapor migrates toward the condensation zone, where it condenses and crystallizes in a region with suitable temperature conditions. The heating and condensation zones are both situated within the internally insulated furnace body. The thermal insulation performance of the furnace is ensured by thermal insulation refractory that fully line the chamber walls, thereby maintaining a uniform temperature distribution throughout the furnace. The temperature variation along the horizontal axis, defined as the temperature gradient, was quantitatively determined using an array of thermocouples. Experimental measurements revealed that within the investigated temperature range of 700–900 °C, the axial temperature gradient from the heating volatilization zone and condensation region increased approximately linearly from 18.5 °C/cm to 22 °C/cm with increasing gasification temperatures.
After the holding stage, the furnace was allowed to cool to room temperature, at which point the vacuum pump is turned off, and the system vacuum is released. To prevent rapid oxidation, the residue of RE richment is immediately transferred to a glove box filled with an Ar protective atmosphere. Finally, both the condensed Mg metal on the graphite paper and the RE richment are collected for subsequent analysis and characterization.
The mass of the recycling products was measured, and the elemental composition of the samples was analyzed by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP–AES, OPTIMA 8000, PerkinElmer Corporation, USA). Microstructure observations and element distribution analyses were performed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, ZEISS Sigma 300, Germany) coupled with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, Oxford Xplore 30, UK). The crystal structure of the condensed Mg at different temperatures was studied by X–ray diffraction (XRD, SmartLab SE, Rigaku, Japan; test range: 5–90°, sweep speed: 2°/min, light source: Cu–Kα rays, tube voltage: 40 kV, current: 40 mA). The volatilization rate and RE element enrichment rate were calculated using Eqs. (1), (2) to evaluate the effect of the vacuum sublimation gasification recycling process:

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Thermodynamic analysis

Due to the high volatility of metal Mg, both its production and recycling processes rely on this characteristic, which can be described using its saturated vapor pressure. The saturated vapor pressure of a metal can be derived from the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, which mathematically expresses the quantitative function relationship between vapor pressure and temperature [35]:(3)lgP∗=A/T+BlgT+CT+Dwhere P∗ is the saturated vapor pressure of pure metal; T is the absolute temperature in K; The parameters A, B, C and D are the evaporation constants for each pure metal, which from Refs. [36,37].
Fig. 3(a) presents the saturated vapor pressures of alloying elements and impurity elements in the ZM6 alloy. It can be seen that the volatilization sequence of metals is observed as Zn > Mg > Mn > Al > Cu > Nd > Fe > Ni > Si > Zr. To quantitatively describe the separation capacity between Mg, Nd and other impurities, the separation coefficient (β) was introduced, which serves as an important parameter for alloy separation during vacuum sublimation gasification process:(4)βMg−i=Pi∗γi/PMg∗γMgwhere βMg-i represents the separation coefficient between Mg and element i, and a value closer to 1 indicates a greater difficulty in separation, while a value further from 1 suggests easier separation. P∗i and P∗Mg denote the saturated vapor pressures of element i and Mg, respectively. γi and γMg are the activity coefficients of element i and Mg at a given temperature and concentration. Considering that Mg and Zn volatilize in the form of sublimation without liquid phase appearing under the recycling conditions, and the melting points of all elements except Al exceed 900 °C (higher than the maximum experimental temperature), these components remain in the solid state throughout the process. Therefore, the activity coefficients are assumed to be 1 for all components in the calculations.
Fig. 3(b) shows the separation coefficients of Mg with nine other elements at different temperatures. Among these elements, the separation coefficient βMg-Zn between Zn and Mg is the closest to 1. This indicates that Zn and Mg tend to volatilize simultaneously into the gas phase, rendering their separation quite difficult. Additionally, an elevation in temperature exacerbates the difficulty of separating these two elements. In contrast, the separation coefficients of other elements, including Nd, are at least five orders of magnitude below 1, particularly for Zr. This indicates that these elements remain in the residue without volatilizing, thus being readily separable from Mg. Moreover, as the temperature increases, the separation coefficients of these elements also increase, signifying that elevated temperatures are disadvantageous for their separation from Mg. However, this effect is significant only for elements with higher content, such as alloying element Mn. Conversely, due to the extremely low concentrations of Al, Cu, Fe and Ni, their impact on this phenomenon is negligible.
Moreover, the element content in the gas phase can also be predicted in accordance with Eq. (5). The corresponding results can be further employed to analyze the temperature-dependent variation in gas phase distribution during vacuum sublimation gasification.(5)Ci,g=(1+CMg,sCi,s·PMg∗Pi∗)−1where Ci,g is the mass fraction of the element i in the gas phase; CMg,s and Ci,s are the mass fractions of Mg and element i in the scrap.
Fig. 4 illustrates the variations in the gas-phase content of alloying elements (Nd, Mn, Zr) and impurity elements (Cu, Fe, Ni) with the temperature and content. These ranges of element contents are determined based on the initial content of different elements in the ZM6 scrap and their final concentrations in the residue. This allows for a quantitative assessment of the tendency of impurity elements to enter the gas phase and their impact during diverse gasification recycling stages at various temperatures.
As the gasification temperature increases, the content of impurity elements in the gas phase exhibits an upward-trending behavior. In the early stage, due to the initially low content of these elements in the scrap, the gas-phase content of Nd and Mn remains about 10−10 wt%, while the contents of Zr and other impurity elements are even lower, at less than 10−13 wt%. Consequently, at this stage, the effect of increasing temperature on their gas-phase content is minimal and can even be considered negligible. As the recycling process progresses, less volatile elements continue to accumulate, leading to a gradual increase in their content within the residue. In the later stage, after almost Mg and Zn has volatilized, the Nd becomes matrix metal. Hence, the residue can be considered as the Nd richment or Nd alloy. At this stage, the effect of temperature on the increase in gas-phase content of elements in the residue is significant. At 900 °C, when Nd reaches 90 wt% in the residue, its gas-phase content exceeds 0.1 ppm, which represents a more than 100-fold increase compared to its concentration at 700 °C. Similarly, when Mn accumulates to 1 wt% in the residue, its gas-phase content reaches 0.27 ppm, which is even higher than that of Nd. This is because Mn has a higher volatility compared to Nd, making it more likely to enter the gas phase under elevated temperatures. In addition, if the gasification process continues, Nd and Mn will continue to accumulate in the gas phase over time and condense with Mg, potentially affecting the purity of the recycled Mg. In contrast, elements such as Zr, Cu, Fe, and Ni exhibit extremely low volatility, and even at the same temperature, their gas-phase concentrations remain significantly lower than 10−10 wt%.
Therefore, it is thermodynamically feasible to recycle Mg and Nd from ZM6 alloy by vacuum sublimation gasification. Moreover,to optimize the recovery efficiency while maintaining high-purity recycled Mg, it is essential to carefully control the gasification temperature and holding time, ensuring complete volatilization of Mg and Zn while minimizing the loss of RE elements and Mn into the gas phase.

3.2. Effect of temperature

In order to study the influence of the gasification temperature on the recycling separation effect of Mg from Nd and other elements, the experiments were carried out under the conditions of vacuum degree 10 Pa,holding time 30 min, processing temperature 700–900 °C (923–1123 K) according to thermodynamic analysis result and the actual recycling process.
Fig. 5(a) shows the relationship between the purity of condensed Mg (i.e. the recycled Mg), volatilization rate and gasification temperature. It can be observed that as temperature increases, both the volatilization rate of the raw material and the purity of the condensed Mg also rises. As previously mentioned, saturated vapor pressure is a function of temperature, and an increase in temperature leads to a rapid rise in the saturated vapor pressures of Mg and Zn, thereby accelerating their volatilization rate. Consequently, when the gasification temperature increases from 700 °C to 850 °C, the volatilization rate significantly increases from 27.70 % to 92.43 %. However, as the temperature continues to rise to 900 °C, the volatilization rate increases slowly to 96.67 %, approaching the theoretical volatilization rate of ZM6 alloy (96.79 %, assuming complete volatilization of Mg and Zn). This phenomenon occurs because as the volatile metals undergo gasification from the outer surface inward, their concentrations progressively decrease, while the less volatile components become dominant. Additionally, volatile metals located in the inner regions may become encapsulated by less volatile metals or experience hindered heat transfer, leading to a slower increase in the overall volatilization rate.
Regarding the purity of condensed Mg, it exhibits a slight increase with rising temperature, increasing from 99.89 % at 700 °C to 99.95 % at 900 °C. This trend is primarily attributed to the reduction in Zn content, which decreases from 0.1 wt% to 0.054 wt% as temperature increases. As previously reported by our research group, Mg and Zn exhibit distinct condensation temperature ranges at 10 Pa: 460–330 °C for Mg [38] and 350–230 °C for Zn [39]. This discrepancy indicates that Zn preferentially condenses in cooler regions and helps explain the differing trends in Zn content compared to other elements in the condensed Mg. However, the observed partial overlap in their condensation ranges suggests potential co-condensation effects in intermediate temperature zones, which may explain the residual zinc content in the final product.
These results indicate that Zn content is the critical factor determining the purity of recycled Mg, but the difficulty of separating Mg and Zn is also widely recognized during the vacuum sublimation gasification recycling process [40]. Furthermore, it is important to note that the concentrations of other less volatile metals in the condensed Mg remain at the ppm level, which has little impact on the purity of condensed Mg. Such a situation may be attributed to the insufficient holding time during the experiment. During the 30 min holding period, the energy absorbed by the waste material was primarily utilized for the volatilization of Mg and Zn, while the volatilization of other less volatile metals lacked sufficient energy support. Therefore, increasing the gasification temperature is beneficial for reducing the Zn content in recycled Mg, thereby enhancing its overall purity.
Fig. 5(b) shows the variation in the content of Nd, Zr, Mn, Al, Zn, Fe, Cu and Ni in the residue with increasing gasification temperature. It can be observed that, except for Zn, the concentrations of other elements increase with rising temperature. This phenomenon is closely related to the change of volatilization rate, as the continuous depletion of the matrix metal Mg results in a relative increase in the concentration of residual elements. When the temperature increases from 700 °C to 900 °C, the Nd content rises from 38.66 wt% to 76.70 wt%, achieving an approximately 29-fold enrichment compared to the original ZM6 scrap. In contrast, Zn, which has a higher saturated vapor pressure and greater volatility than Mg, exhibits a decreasing trend in the residue as temperature increases.
Therefore, increasing the temperature facilitates the volatilization of Mg and Zn from the scrap and enhances their separation from RE element Nd, ultimately obtaining recycled Mg and Nd alloy. The purity of recycled Mg predominantly depends on Zn. The decrease in Zn content with increasing temperature has a positive impact on the purity of recycled Mg, due to its relatively high gas phase content, which overshadows the fact that other alloying and impurity elements enter the gas phase. Moreover, when the gasification temperature is higher than 750 °C, the purity of recycled Mg consistently exceeds 99.9 % with only minor fluctuations.

3.3. Effect of holding time

To achieve optimal recycling results, it is crucial to precisely regulate the recycling process by determining an appropriate holding time. This approach guarantees the complete volatilization and separation of Mg and Zn. Concurrently, it avoids the pollution of recycled Mg and the loss of Nd caused by a large number of alloying elements such as Mn and Nd entering the gas phase. In order to achieve more comprehensive control over the gasification process, the effect of holding time on the purity of recycled Mg and Nd enrichment during ZM6 scrap recycling was studied under the vacuum degree 10 Pa and gasification temperature 750 °C.
The variations in both purity of recycled Mg and volatilization rate of scrap with the holding time are illustrated in Fig. 6(a). In the early stage of the holding process, Mg volatilizes rapidly, with the volatilization rate reaching 52.75 % at 30 min and 86.80 % at 60 min. During this period, the primary volatilization occurs from the Mg solid solution (matrix). After 60 min, as the Mg matrix is progressively depleted, the Mg in the compounds is decomposed, released and volatilized, leading to a slower increase in the volatilization rate. When the holding time reaches 120 min, the volatilization rate stabilizes at 96.93 %, which is very close to the theoretical volatilization rate of 96.79 % (corresponding to the complete volatilization of Mg and Zn). This result indicates that the Mg and Zn in the ZM6 scrap have almost completely volatilized.
Similarly, the purity of recycled Mg in the condensation zone is also determined by the Zn content. As shown in the bar chart of Fig. 6(a), the purity of the recycled Mg is between 99.914 and 99.946 wt%, while the concentrations of other impurity metals remain at approximately 2 ppm. The slight variations in purity are attributed to fluctuations in Zn content, which fall within the range of normal experimental error. This result is similar to the effect of temperature on the purity of recycled Mg. Since Mg volatilization occurs through sublimation, the gasification process can be considered as proceeding layer by layer. As evidenced by the elemental distribution map of the scrap presented in Fig. 1(c), the alloy composition exhibits a homogeneous distribution, indicating that the Zn content is approximately uniform across each layer. Therefore, at the same gasification temperature, the Zn content in recycled Mg is minimally affected by the holding time, fluctuating around 0.07 wt%. It can be seen from Fig. 6(b) that the contents of Nd, Zr, and Mn in the residue significantly increase with the with the extension of the holding time. After 120 min of vacuum sublimation gasification recycling, the Nd content in the residue reaches 83.84 wt%, achieving an enrichment factor of 31.76. Meanwhile, the content of impurity elements Cu, Fe, Ni also increased slightly. Further extending the holding time does not increase the Nd content. Instead, it may cause potential contamination of the condensed Mg.
When comprehensively considering factors including product purity, separation performance, and the controllability of the recycling process, the optimal recycling conditions are identified. These conditions involve a gasification temperature of 750 °C and a holding time of 120 min. Under such conditions, the volatilization rate attains 96.93 %, the purity of recycled Mg reaches 99.936 wt%, and the purity of Nd is 83.84 wt%.

3.4. Morphology analysis

Under a vacuum pressure of 10 Pa, metal vapor migrates to the condensation zone, where it becomes supersaturated and subsequently condenses on the graphite paper. The condensation behavior of Mg has been extensively studied in previous research [38], indicating that variations in gasification temperature do not affect the condensation temperature of the Mg vapor. Hence, the condensed Mg obtained at 700 °C was selected as an example for analysis. The condensed Mg was sectioned from the high-temperature to the low-temperature condensation zone at intervals of 3 cm, resulting in samples labeled 1# to 4#, as shown in Fig. 7. By correlating the condensation position with the corresponding temperature, it was determined that the initial and final condensation temperatures of the recycled Mg were 521 °C and 270 °C, respectively. This condensation temperature range is wider than the research results obtained by Xiong et al. [38]. This is due to the increase in the mass of the experimental sample, which leads to an increase in the mass of Mg vapor and the release of energy during condensation.
From the microstructure of the SEM images in Fig. 7, it can be observed that the condensed Mg of sample 1# exhibits large, dense crystals with regular shapes and smooth surfaces. This morphology distinctly differs from the droplet-like structures typically formed during liquid condensation, indicating that the condensation of Mg vapor occurs through a sublimation process. With the decrease of the condensation temperature, the grain size of the condensed Mg gradually reduces, and the average particle sizes of 1# to 3# are 280.61 μm, 102.05 μm, and 15.58 μm. Moreover, the surface contour begins to blur, and there are stepped terraces on the surface. This is because as the Mg vapor migrates towards positions with lower temperatures, the reduction in both Mg vapor partial pressure and temperature weakens the driving force for condensation. As a result, the crystallization growth is insufficient, which causes the size of the condensed Mg to decrease and the surface to become rough. Microstructural characterization of the condensates in the terminal condensation zone revealed ultrafine particulate formations with a mean diameter of 0.5 μm, exhibiting agglomerated morphologies characterized by pseudospherical granular assemblies. Based on the analysis of the mass distribution proportion of the condensates, it can be concluded that the proportion of the condensate mass distribution shows a rapid downward trend as the condensation temperature decreases. The condensate of sample 1# exhibits the optimal crystallization state, with its mass proportion reaching as high as 61.01 %. In contrast, the mass proportions of the condensates from sample 2# and sample 3# decrease successively to 32.58 % and 5.84 %, respectively. The mass proportion of the condensate of sample 4# is the lowest, merely 0.56 %. Meanwhile, XRD analysis reveals that the condensation product consists solely of Mg, with the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) crystal structure of Mg primarily oriented along the [001] direction, followed by the [103] direction. The carbon sources detected in samples 3# and 4# originated from the graphite paper backing the samples. Notably, sample 4# exhibited significantly higher characteristic carbon peaks than Mg peaks due to its low condensate mass, which aligns with the mass distribution results. Additionally, element mapping analyses of Mg indicate that the Zn content in the condensate gradually increases and distributes uniformly as the condensation temperature decreases. This observation is consistent with previous findings that Zn tends to condense in regions with lower temperatures. Therefore, a relatively high condensation temperature is conducive to obtaining recycled condensed Mg with dense crystallization, high mass proportion, and purity.
The separation of Mg and Zn represents a critical challenge in vacuum-based recycling of magnesium alloy scrap, as Zn is the second most prevalent alloying element in commercial Mg alloys. This technical barrier directly impacts the economic viability of recycling processes and demands urgent resolution to facilitate sustainable magnesium circular economy. Current research reveals that the separation dilemma originates from two key aspects: (1) Zn preferentially volatilizes ahead of magnesium and co-condenses with Mg; (2) their condensation temperature ranges partially overlap during the condensation stage. One strategy is adjusting the pressure in vacuum distillation to enable sequential volatilization (Zn first, followed by Mg). However, the recovery efficiency is severely limited by the low volatilization rate. Another promising strategy involves regulating operational conditions (e.g., condensation temperature, pressure, condensing medium, nucleation agents) to amplify the condensation behavior differences between the two metals, which necessitates further investigation into the condensation characteristics of Mg and Zn.
Fig. 8 presents the physical images, surface microstructure and mass distribution maps of the residues obtained at different temperatures. Under a constant holding time, the residue formed at 700 °C exhibits a continuous porous network structure (Fig. 8(a)). EDS analysis confirms that the primary components of the residue are Nd and Zr, with only 4 wt% Mg and 0.22 wt% Zn remaining unvolatilized. This observation correlates well with the initial microstructure of the raw material, where Nd and Zr, initially uniformly distributed within the alloy, form a network-like framework after the volatilization of Mg and Zn. However, there's still a lot of unvolatilized Mg inside the residue.
As the temperature increases, the volatilization of Mg and Zn intensifies, leading to a reduction in the volume of the residue. The changes in microstructure provide further insight into this phenomenon. At 800 °C, as shown in Fig. 8(b), the network structure begins to soften and collapse inward, causing the residues to stack upon each other. This structural collapse can encapsulate the remaining Mg, hindering its volatilization. This observation supports the earlier conclusion that the volatilization rate slows as Mg becomes trapped within the residue. When the temperature reaches 900 °C, which is close to the melting point of Nd (1021 °C), the residue becomes dense and compact, with no visible pores or gaps on the surface, as shown in Fig. 8(c). At this time, Mg and Zn have tended to volatilize completely according to the EDS results.
Therefore, by controlling the gasification temperature, the morphology of the Nd-rich alloy can be adjusted to meet different recycling or reuse requirements. At lower temperatures, the Nd residues recovered exhibit a porous and loose structure, which facilitates the complete removal of Mg and Zn. Additionally, this structural characteristic is advantageous for subsequent processing, such as powder or block preparation, enabling the reuse of these Nd alloys in the production of RE alloys. However, it is crucial to note that the porous Nd richment possesses a significantly high specific surface area, rendering it highly susceptible to oxidation. Therefore, immediate protection with an inert protective gas to avoid oxidation is essential. At higher temperatures, in contrast, the recovered Nd richment is denser and more compact, which facilitates storage, transportation, and subsequent reuse. Nevertheless, the formation of such a dense layer may lead to incomplete removal of Mg and Zn or cause splashing of the residues, potentially resulting in the loss of Nd element.

4. Conclusions

This study investigates the feasibility of recycling the ZM6 scrap using the vacuum sublimation gasification method through thermodynamic analysis. Experimental studies were conducted to evaluate the effects of the gasification recovery process on the purity of recycled Mg and the enrichment of RE elements. The following conclusions were drawn.
  • (1)
    Thermodynamic analysis confirms that it is feasible of separating and recycling Mg and Nd from ZM6 scrap via vacuum sublimation gasification. Under vacuum, metallic Mg is capable of being separated from alloying elements (Mn, Zr) and impurity elements (Al, Cu, Fe, Ni, Si). Zn entirely enters the gas phase and condenses concomitantly with Mg. Meanwhile, the Nd accumulates and enriches in the residue, thereby forming Nd-rich alloy. Moreover, it must also be acknowledged that kinetic factors (such as volatilization rate change, activation energy, restrictive steps) could affect the separation efficiency.
  • (2)
    Under the optimal gasification-recycling conditions of pressure 10 Pa, gasification temperature 750 °C and holding time 120 min, the recycled Mg with a purity of 99.936 % was obtained. Additionally, rare earth Nd was enriched by 31 times, reaching a purity of 83.84 %.
  • (3)
    The purity of recycled Mg is primarily determined by its Zn content, and the separation of Mg and Zn remains a significant challenge. Meanwhile, it is essential to properly control the recycling process to avoid the contamination of recycled Mg resulting from the enrichment of alloying elements Nd and Mn in the residue.
  • (4)
    By regulating the distillation temperature, the morphology of Nd-enriched alloys can be tailored. At 700 °C, a porous and loose structure of RE is obtained, while at 900 °C, a dense bulk form of RE is achieved, facilitating the reuse of Nd.
